claim: New psychoactive substances (NPS) targeting human cannabinoid receptor 1 pose a significant threat to society as recreational abusive drugs that have pronounced physiological side effects.
source: New psychoactive substances (NPS) targeting human cannabinoid receptor 1 pose a significant threat to society as recreational abusive drugs that have pronounced physiological side effects.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that characterizes NPS as a societal threat based on their physiological effects.

claim: Greater adverse effects of NPS compared to classical cannabinoids have been linked to higher downstream β-arrestin signaling.
source: These greater adverse effects compared to classical cannabinoids have been linked to the higher downstream β-arrestin signaling.
evidence: This statement references prior research linking adverse effects to β-arrestin signaling.

claim: Cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB1) is majorly expressed in the central nervous system (CNS) and belongs to the class A G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) family proteins.
source: Cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB1), which is majorly expressed in the central nervous system (CNS) belongs to the class A G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) family proteins (Hua et al., 2016; Mackie, 2008; Zou and Kumar, 2018; Dutta and Shukla, 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: GPCRs are expressed in the cellular membrane and help transduce chemical signals from the extracellular to the intracellular direction with the help of downstream signaling proteins (G-proteins and β-arrestin).
source: GPCRs are expressed in the cellular membrane and help transduce chemical signals from the extracellular to the intracellular direction with the help of the downstream signaling proteins (G-proteins and β-arrestin) (Rosenbaum et al., 2009; Latorraca et al., 2017; Weis and Kobilka, 2018).
evidence: This statement describes GPCR function and is supported by citations.

claim: GPCRs are the largest family of drug targets due to their substantial involvement in human pathophysiology and druggability.
source: In addition, GPCRs are the largest family of drug targets due to their substantial involvement in human pathophysiology and druggability (Hauser et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: HU-210 is a Schedule I controlled substance in the United States.
source: One such example of a synthetic cannabinoid is 1,1-Dimethylheptyl-11-hydroxy-tetrahydrocannabinol (commonly known as HU-210), which is a Schedule I controlled substance in the United States (Farinha-Ferreira et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: NPS synthetic cannabinoids consist of four pharmacophore components: linked, linker, core, and tail groups.
source: The molecular structures of NPS synthetic cannabinoids consist of four pharmacophore components: linked, linker, core, and tail groups (Worob and Wenthur, 2020; Potts et al., 2020).
evidence: This structural description is supported by citations.

claim: The core of NPS synthetic cannabinoids usually consists of aromatic scaffolds such as indole, indazole, carbazole, and benzimidazole.
source: The core usually consists of aromatic scaffolds (e.g. indole, indazole, carbazole, benzimidazole) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Schoeder et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and reference to a figure.

claim: Use of NPS synthetic cannabinoids has been found to cause more physiological side effects than traditional cannabinergic 'tetrad' side effects.
source: The use of NPS synthetic cannabinoids has been found to cause more physiological side effects than traditional cannabinergic 'tetrad' side effects (Tai and Fantegrossi, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: NPS side effects include tachycardia, drowsiness, dizziness, hypertension, seizures, convulsions, nausea, high blood pressure, and chest pain.
source: These side effects include tachycardia, drowsiness, dizziness, hypertension, seizures, convulsions, nausea, high blood pressure, and chest pain (Tai and Fantegrossi, 2014; Finlay et al., 2019).
evidence: This list of side effects is supported by citations.

claim: High concentrations of AMB-FUBINACA induced tremors.
source: For instance, Gatch and Forster have shown that the high concentrations of AMB-FUBINACA, the molecule which caused 'zombie outbreak' in New York, induced tremors (Gatch and Forster, 2019; Adams et al., 2017).
evidence: This specific finding is supported by citations.

claim: A recent biochemical study has linked discriminatory effects of NPS with differential signaling of β-arrestin.
source: A recent biochemical study has linked these discriminatory effects with the differential signaling of β-arrestin (Finlay et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement references a specific study linking effects to β-arrestin signaling.

claim: NPS shows higher β-arrestin signaling compared to classical cannabinoids.
source: According to Finlay et al., NPS shows higher β-arrestin signaling compared to the classical cannabinoids, which has also been confirmed by other β-arrestin signaling studies (Finlay et al., 2019; Grafinger et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mutagenesis studies have shown that the conserved NPxxY motif of CB1 has a larger role in downstream β-arrestin signaling than G-protein signaling.
source: Mutagenesis studies have shown that the conserved NPxxY motif of CB1 have a larger role in downstream β-arrestin signaling than G-protein signaling (Leo et al., 2023; Liao et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to mutagenesis studies.

claim: Recently published MDMB-FUBINACA bound CB1-β-arrestin-1 complex structure points out the importance of the unique triad interaction (Y3977.53-Y2945.58-T2103.46) involving NPxxY motif in β-arrestin-1 signaling.
source: Recently published MDMB-FUBINACA bound CB1-β-arrestin-1 complex structure also points out the importance of the unique triad interaction (Y3977.53-Y2945.58-T2103.46) involving NPxxY motif in β-arrestin-1 signaling (Liao et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement references a recently published structure and is supported by a citation.

claim: Structural comparison of classical cannabinoid (AM841) and NPS (MDMB-FUBINACA) bound active CB1-Gi complex shows a conformationally similar NPxxY motif.
source: However, structural comparison of the classical cannabinoid (AM841) and NPS (MDMB-FUBINACA) bound active CB1-Gi complex shows a conformationally similar NPxxY motif (Figure 2; Krishna Kumar et al., 2019; Hua et al., 2020).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations and reference to Figure 2.

claim: Higher β-arrestin signaling stems from higher dynamic propensity of triad interaction formation for NPS-bound CB1.
source: In light of these experimental observations, it can be inferred that higher β-arrestin signaling stems from higher dynamic propensity of triad interaction formation for NPS-bound CB1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental observations.

claim: Distinct orthosteric pocket interactions for NPS and classical cannabinoids cause differential allosteric modulation of intracellular dynamics that facilitate triad interaction.
source: We hypothesized that distinct orthosteric pocket interactions for NPS and classical cannabinoids cause differential allosteric modulation of intracellular dynamics that facilitate triad interaction.
evidence: This is the stated hypothesis of the study.

claim: MDMB-FUBINACA has a Ki of 1.14 nM.
source: These ligands binds to CB1 receptor with nanomolar affinities (MDMB-FUBINACA Ki: 1.14 nM; Gamage et al., 2018; HU-210 Ki: 0.61 nM Pertwee et al., 2010; Stern and Lambert, 2007).
evidence: This binding affinity value is supported by a citation.

claim: HU-210 has a Ki of 0.61 nM.
source: These ligands binds to CB1 receptor with nanomolar affinities (MDMB-FUBINACA Ki: 1.14 nM; Gamage et al., 2018; HU-210 Ki: 0.61 nM Pertwee et al., 2010; Stern and Lambert, 2007).
evidence: This binding affinity value is supported by citations.

claim: Two replicas of well-tempered metadynamics were performed to capture the unbinding pathways of MDMB-FUBINACA and HU-210.
source: Here, two replicas of well-tempered metadynamics were performed to capture the unbinding pathways of MDMB-FUBINACA and HU-210 from the ligand-bound receptors, whose starting structures were obtained from a cryo-EM complex (PDB ID: 6N4B Krishna Kumar et al., 2019) and docking, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the computational methods used in the study.

claim: Ligands follow a similar pathway for each replica in metadynamics simulations.
source: The z-component distance was plotted against the RMSD of the ligands from the bound pose, which indicates that ligands follow a similar pathway for each replica (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and C).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: Dissociation happens via the opening formed by TM2, TM3, ECL2, and N-terminus for both ligands.
source: It is observed that the dissociation happens via the opening formed by TM2, TM3, ECL2, and N-terminus for both ligands (Figure 3).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: MSM and TRAM predictions of standard binding free energy are within 0.6 kcal/mol of each other for each ligand.
source: TRAM and MSM predictions of standard binding free energy are within 0.6 kcal/mol of each other for each ligand (Figure 4A).
evidence: This comparison is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The relative estimated free energy (ΔΔG) values are within 0.6 kcal/mol of the experimentally determined values.
source: Although the absolute binding free energy differs from the experimentally predicted value by approximately 3 kcal/mol, the relative estimated free energy (ΔΔG) values are also within 0.6 kcal/mol of the experimentally determined values (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This comparison to experimental values is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: Estimated binding times using TRAM and MSM match perfectly for both ligands.
source: Estimated binding times using TRAM and MSM match perfectly for both ligands (Figure 4B).
evidence: This comparison is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The estimated dissociation times are within one order of magnitude with each other.
source: The estimated dissociation times are within one order of magnitude with each other (Figure 4C).
evidence: This comparison is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: With only 25% of original unbiased data, TRAM can predict the kinetics within an order magnitude of the kinetics estimated with full dataset.
source: It is observed that even with only 25% of original, unbiased data, TRAM can predict the kinetics within an order magnitude of the kinetics estimated with full dataset (Figure 4D).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Error in MSM predicted kinetics increases more rapidly compared to TRAM with lesser amount of unbiased data.
source: On the other hand, error in MSM predicted kinetics more rapidly compared to TRAM with lesser amount of unbiased data.
evidence: This comparison is based on the data analysis performed in the study.

claim: TRAM provides better predictions of thermodynamics and kinetics when less amount of unbiased data.
source: Therefore, TRAM provides better predictions of thermodynamics and kinetics when less amount of unbiased data.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparative analysis of TRAM and MSM.

claim: In the bound pose of MDMB-FUBINACA, major interactions form between aromatic (F1702.57, W2795.43, F268ECL2) and hydrophobic (L1933.29) residues of the binding pocket.
source: In the bound pose, the major interactions form between the aromatic (F1702.57, W2795.43, F268ECL2) and hydrophobic (L1933.29) residues of the binding pocket (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: For MDMB-FUBINACA, the aromatic tail part moves away from TM5 and forms interactions with aromatic residues in TM2 (F1702.57 and F1742.61) in one unbinding pathway.
source: One of the pathways, aromatic tail part of MDMB-FUBINACA moves away from TM5 and forms interactions with aromatic residues in TM2 (F1702.57 and F1742.61) (Figures 5A and 6A, B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The transition from bound pose to I1 has a timescale of 20.6±2.3 μs for MDMB-FUBINACA.
source: MFPT calculations show that both the timescales are similar with slightly higher timescales for the bound pose compared to I1 transition (20.6±2.3 μs) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This timescale is calculated from MFPT analysis and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The transition from I1 to I3 (33.7±3.1 μs) is much slower compared to reverse transition (0.8±0.0 μs) for MDMB-FUBINACA.
source: Kinetically, the transition from I1 to I3 (33.7±3.1 μs) is much slower compared to reverse transition (0.8±0.0 μs), validating the higher stability of the I1 compared to I3 macrostate (Figure 6B).
evidence: These timescales are calculated from MFPT analysis and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Breaking the aromatic interactions for complete dissociation of MDMB-FUBINACA requires ∼371.9±40.2 μs, making it the slowest step in this pathway.
source: According to the TPT analysis, breaking the aromatic interactions for complete dissociation of MDMB-FUBINACA requires ∼371.9±40.2 μs, making it the slowest step in this pathway (Figure 6B).
evidence: This timescale is calculated from TPT analysis and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Classical cannabinoid HU-210 shows higher interactions with TM7 residues (S3837.39, F3797.35) compared to MDMB-FUBINACA.
source: Comparing the bound macrostate interactions of MDMB-FUBINACA, classical cannabinoid HU-210 shows higher interactions with TM7 residues (S3837.39, F3797.35) (Figures 6A and 7A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This comparison is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Experimentally determined structures of classical cannabinoid bound CB1 have pointed out conserved polar interactions of the hydroxyl group at C-1 position with S3837.39.
source: Previous experimentally determined structures of classical cannabinoid bound CB1 have pointed out these conserved polar interactions of the hydroxyl group at C-1 position with S3837.39 (Hua et al., 2020; Hua et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental structures.

claim: Although MDMB-FUBINACA also maintains polar interaction with carboxylic oxygen, the interaction energy for HU-210 is much higher.
source: Although MDMB-FUBINACA also maintain this polar interaction with carboxylic oxygen, the interaction energy for the HU-210 is much higher, depicting the importance of this conserved residue in stabilizing classical cannabinoids (Figure 6B).
evidence: This comparison is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Alanine mutation of S3837.39 has been shown to decrease the ligand affinity and downstream efficacy of classical cannabinoids by orders of magnitude.
source: Alanine mutation of S3837.39 have shown to decrease the ligand affinity and downstream efficacy of classical cannabinoids by orders of magnitude, while having minimal effect on WIN-55,212–2, which have carboxylic oxygen in the linked part as MDMB-FUBINACA (Kapur et al., 2007; Sitkoff et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to mutagenesis studies.

claim: In the I1 macrostate of HU-210, the hydroxyl group at C-11 forms a major polar interaction with H1782.65.
source: Protein-ligand interaction analysis in the macrostate representing this region (I1) shows that hydroxyl group at C-11 forms a major polar interaction with H1782.65 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: For HU-210, breaking of polar interaction with S3837.39 and hydrophobic interaction with F1702.57 leads to larger kinetic barrier of approximately 39.5±1.4 μs.
source: Major interactions that break when the ligand moves out of the binding pose to macrostate I2 is the polar interaction with S3837.39 and hydrophobic interaction with aromatic F1702.57 (Figure 7A and B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C). Breaking of these bonds leads to larger kinetic barrier of approximately 39.5±1.4 μs (Figure 7B).
evidence: This timescale is calculated from analysis and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: From both I2 and I3 macrostates, HU-210 can dissociate from the pocket with mean free passage time in the millisecond timescale, which is one order of magnitude higher compared to MDMB-FUBINACA unbinding.
source: From both I2 and I3 macrostates, the ligand can dissociate from the pocket and mean free passage time for these transitions appear to be in the millisecond timescale, which is one order of magnitude higher compared to the MDMB-FUBINACA unbinding (Figure 6B).
evidence: This comparison is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Larger mean distance between carbonyl oxygen of NPS molecules' linker group and S3837.39 compared to equivalent distance of hydroxyl group of classical cannabinoids' benzopyran ring supports the universality of weaker interaction between TM7 and NPS molecules.
source: Average distance of carbonyl oxygen of NPS molecules' linker group from S3837.39 is compared to equivalent distance of hydroxyl group of classical cannabinoids' benzopyran ring. Larger mean distance in case of all NPS-bound CB1 supports the universality of the weaker interaction between TM7 and NPS molecules (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Each binding pocket residue in MDMB-FUBINACA bound ensemble shows higher allosteric weights with the NPxxY motif compared to HU-210, indicating larger dynamic interactions between the NPxxY motif and binding pocket residues.
source: Results show that each binding pocket residue in MDMB-FUBINACA bound ensemble shows higher allosteric weights with the NPxxY motif, indicating larger dynamic interactions between the NPxxY motif and binding pocket residues (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This observation is supported by data from NRI analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mutual information analysis reaffirms that allosteric weights between binding pocket and NPxxY motif residues are higher for the MDMB-FUBINACA bound ensemble.
source: To further validate our observations, we estimated allosteric weights between the binding pocket and the NPxxY motif by calculating mutual information between residue movements. Mutual information analysis reaffirms that allosteric weights between these residues are indeed higher for the MDMB-FUBINACA bound ensemble (Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This validation is supported by mutual information analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: TRAM weighted probability calculation showed that MDMB-FUBINACA bound CB1 has the higher probability of triad formation compared to HU-210.
source: TRAM weighted probability calculation showed that MDMB-FUBINACA bound CB1 has the higher probability of triad formation (Figure 8A).
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Interaction between Y3977.53-T2103.46 is relatively more stable in case of MDMB-FUBINACA bound CB1, while other two interactions have similar behavior for both systems.
source: Comparison of the pairwise interaction of the triad residues shows that interaction between Y3977.53-T2103.46 is relatively more stable in case of MDMB-FUBINACA bound CB1, while other two interactions have similar behavior for both systems (Figure 8—figure supplement 5A, B, and C).
evidence: This comparison is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 5.

claim: Higher interaction between Y3977.53 and T2103.46 in MDMB-FUBINACA bound receptor causes the triad interaction to be more probable.
source: Therefore, higher interaction between Y3977.53 and T2103.46 in MDMB-FUBINACA bound receptor causes the triad interaction to be more probable.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the pairwise interaction analysis.

claim: Well-tempered metadynamics simulations were able to find similar pathways via the opening formed by TM2, TM3, N-terminus, and ECL2 which matches with previous metadynamics binding simulations for cannabinoid receptors.
source: These simulations were able to find similar pathways via the opening formed by TM2, TM3, N-terminus, and ECL2 which matches with previous metadynamics binding simulations for cannabinoid receptors.
evidence: This observation is compared to previous simulation studies.

claim: The pathway may be the minimum free energy pathway for the ligand unbinding in CB1.
source: These observations indicate that the pathway may be the minimum free energy pathway for the ligand unbinding in CB1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that ligands follow similar pathways in multiple simulations.

claim: Aromatic residues in the pocket (F2688ECL2, F1702.57) form major interactions with both HU-210 and MDMB-FUBINACA.
source: Third, aromatic residues in the pocket (F2688ECL2, F1702.57) form major interactions with both HU-210 and MDMB-FUBINACA.
evidence: This observation is based on the interaction analysis performed in the study.

claim: Major differences in protein-ligand interactions were observed in TM7, with stronger interactions for classical cannabinoid HU-210 with TM7, especially polar interaction with S3837.39 and hydrophobic interaction with F3797.35 compared to MDMB-FUBINACA.
source: Major differences in protein-ligand interactions were observed in TM7. Stronger interactions were observed for the classical cannabinoid HU-210 with TM7, especially polar interaction with S3837.39 and hydrophobic interaction with F3797.35 compared to MDMB-FUBINACA.
evidence: This observation is based on the interaction analysis performed in the study.

claim: This interaction pattern was consistent across other NPS and classical cannabinoids, indicating a universal difference in how these two groups of compounds interact with TM7.
source: This interaction pattern was consistent across other NPS and classical cannabinoids, indicating a universal difference in how these two groups of compounds interact with TM7.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the analysis of multiple NPS and classical cannabinoid simulations.

claim: Higher allosteric weights from the binding pocket residues to the NPxxY motif region for MDMB-FUBINACA bound CB1 increases the probability of triad interaction formation.
source: Dynamic allostery measured by the posterior probability of VAE shows that higher allosteric weights from the binding pocket residues to the NPxxY motif region for MDMB-FUBINACA bound CB1 increases the probability of triad interaction formation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the NRI analysis and triad formation probability data.

claim: Missing residues in ICL3 (21 residues, 314–334) and ECL2 (6 residues, 258–263) were modeled sequentially using Remodel protocol of Rosetta loop modeling.
source: Missing residues in ICL3 (21 residues, 314–334) and ECL2 (6 residues, 258–263) were modeled sequentially using Remodel protocol of Rosetta loop modeling (Stein and Kortemme, 2013; Alford et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the modeling methods used in the study.

claim: The closest 20 residues of N-terminus were modeled as membrane proximal regions of the N-terminus were shown to be important for CB1 signaling by allosterically modulating ligand affinity.
source: Therefore, the closest 20 residues were modeled as membrane proximal regions of the N-terminus were shown to be important for CB1 signaling by allosterically modulating ligand affinity (Fay and Farrens, 2013).
evidence: This modeling decision is supported by a citation.

claim: An average brain membrane composition of asymmetric complex membrane was selected for the simulations.
source: As CB1 is majorly expressed in central nervous system, an average brain membrane composition of asymmetric complex membrane was selected.
evidence: This describes the simulation setup.

claim: The membrane composition was obtained from Ingólfsson et al. and proportionally downsized according to the system.
source: The membrane composition was obtained from Ingólfsson et al. and proportionally downsized according to our system (Table 1; Ingólfsson et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the membrane composition used and is supported by a citation and table.

claim: CHARMM36m force field was used to parameterize the protein, lipid, water, and ions.
source: CHARMM36m force field was used to parameterize the protein, lipid, water, and ions (Huang et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the force field used and is supported by a citation.

claim: The docked bound pose of HU-210 was selected based on best overall structure to the experimentally determined crystal structure of another bound classical cannabinoid (Ligand: AM841, PDB:6KPG).
source: The docked bound pose was selected based on best overall structure of HU-210 to the experimentally determined crystal structure of another bound classical cannabinoid (Ligand: AM841, PDB:6KPG Hua et al., 2020; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the docking procedure and is supported by a citation and figure reference.
